progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c11 (a buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base, both in large amounts; the conjugate base takes up added hydronium and the weak acid takes up added hydroxide; [H₃O⁺] = Ka × n(HA) ÷ n(A⁻) with moles because the volume cancels; equal amounts give pH = pKa; capacity depends on the amounts). chem-m6-c10 (ethanoic acid Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, pKa 4.74). chem-m6-c07 (pH from [H₃O⁺]; the decimal-places rule). chem-m6-p03 (the meter routine; open distilled water reads near 5.9 because of dissolved CO₂). chem-m6-p04 (tenfold dilution with a volumetric pipette and flask; a strong acid's pH moves about one unit, 0.96 in its class data). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy; variables; risk). Year 11: n = c × V.
progression.startsWith: Prepare a weak acid and conjugate base mixture. The video opens: These two beakers both read pH four point six eight. One is a buffer you've just made. The other is very dilute hydrochloric acid.
progression.stopsAfter: choosing a buffer pair and amounts for a target pH near pKa; preparing about 100 mL accurately and making enough for every test; predicting and measuring its pH and explaining a small difference; designing tests with a water control, the same dose and separate fresh portions; comparing pH changes for added acid and base; explaining the acid result with the ratio; showing that dilution barely changes the pH but cuts the capacity; naming the variables; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows. No Henderson-Hasselbalch log form, no partial-neutralisation preparation (chem-m6-c14), no capacity curve (chem-m6-c11), no blood buffers (chem-m6-c11).
progression.nextLesson: direct titration to find an unknown concentration (route chem-m6-c12).

teaching.task: Two beakers both read pH 4.68: one is a buffer you've just made, the other is very dilute hydrochloric acid. How do you prepare a buffer, and what tests prove that it behaves like one?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) same pH, so which is the buffer? You must test what it does (1); (2) a weak acid and its conjugate base in equal moles, so the pH should be close to pKa, 4.74 (2); (3) accurate volumes, because the ratio sets the pH; enough solution for every test (3); (4) measured 4.68, a little below prediction, because real ions affect each other and stocks aren't perfect; the practical compares changes (4); (5) split into fresh 20.0 mL portions with water controls; the same 1.00 mL dose; acid and base in separate portions, because base added after acid would just undo the acid (5); (6) the buffer moves less than a tenth of a unit; water moves 3.58 and 5.70 units (from 5.93, because of dissolved CO₂, P03) (6); (7) why: the dose is a tenth of the ethanoate, so the ratio moves from 1 to about 1.2 and the predicted pH from 4.74 to 4.66, the same small drop as measured (7); (8) dilute tenfold: both partners dilute equally, so the ratio and the pH barely change (4.68 to 4.72) (8); (9) but the diluted portion holds a tenth of the partners, and the same dose uses up all its ethanoate: the pH falls to 3.41; capacity depends on amounts (9); variables (10); validity, reliability, accuracy (11); risk (12); memory aid (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two beakers both read pH 4.68, one a buffer just made and one very dilute hydrochloric acid, so the practical asks how to prepare a buffer and which tests prove that it behaves like one. The pair (ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate) and the amounts come from the buffers video, the buffer is made with volumetric pipettes in a batch large enough to split, and its measured pH is compared with the ratio prediction. The test is designed with fresh 20 mL portions, a water control given the same dose, and acid and base additions; the results show the buffer moving under a tenth of a unit while the water moves by units, and the C11 ratio calculation shows why. Dilution leaves the ratio, and so the pH, nearly unchanged, while capacity falls because a tenth of the partners is used up by the same dose. The variables, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow, and the memory aid is "Split. Dose. Compare." Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: These two beakers both read pH four point six eight. One is a buffer you've just made. The other is very dilute hydrochloric acid. Which is which? You can't tell from the reading, because a buffer isn't defined by its pH. It's defined by what it does. So in this practical you'll make a buffer, and then prove it.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student tests whether a solution is a buffer. She adds 1.00 mL of 0.100 mol/L hydrochloric acid to 20.0 mL of the solution, and the pH changes from 4.68 to 4.59. She then adds 1.00 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide to the same beaker, and the pH returns to 4.68. She concludes that the solution is a buffer that resists both acid and base. Evaluate her method." Answer: the small change is consistent with a buffer, but (1) there is no control: the same additions to 20.0 mL of water are needed to show the change is unusually small; (2) the base was added to the beaker that already held the acid, so it just neutralised that acid and the return to 4.68 shows nothing about resisting base; use a fresh portion. Crossed mistake: "the pH came back, so it resists base too". (A2) "A student mixes 30.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L ethanoic acid with 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium ethanoate at 25 °C. Calculate the expected pH of the mixture. Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵." Answer: n(CH₃COOH) = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol, n(CH₃COO⁻) = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol; [H₃O⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 3.00 = 5.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L; pH 4.27. Crossed mistake: "pH = pKa = 4.74" (true only for equal amounts).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to prepare a buffer and demonstrate its properties (ACSCH080)" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the buffer practical; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: choosing the pair and the amounts (ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate in equal moles, so the pH should sit near pKa, a C11 callback); preparing about 100 mL with volumetric pipettes (the pipettes fix the moles) and making enough for every test; measuring its pH and comparing it with the prediction; testing four properties with a water control: resisting a small addition of acid, resisting a small addition of base (each in its own fresh portion), resisting dilution, and limited capacity (the diluted buffer and the same dose); explaining the acid result with C11's [H₃O⁺] = Ka × n(HA) ÷ n(A⁻); the variables; validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment. Placement (playlist order 17): after C07 (pH calculation), C08 (weak acids stay mostly un-ionised), C10 (Ka, pKa) and C11 (buffers), so pH calculations and C11's ratio method are used, not re-taught. Not re-taught: why the conjugate base takes up hydronium and the weak acid takes up hydroxide, the two equations, why a strong acid with its salt is not a buffer, blood buffers (all C11; recalled in one clause each where needed). Not here: the Henderson-Hasselbalch log form (C11 decided to leave it out); preparing a buffer by partial neutralisation (chem-m6-c14); a dropwise capacity curve (C11 scene 8 shows it; this video demonstrates capacity with one test instead); buffer range "pKa ± 1".

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C11, P03): ethanoic acid amber, ethanoate grey-violet (C11 ratio bar), hydronium teal, hydroxide violet; readout amber digits; buffer beakers marked with a teal-grey tab, water beakers grey; buffer change bars teal, water change bars pale blue; controls green, hazards terracotta. Board layout (three zones, constant): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the glassware, the beaker grid and the meter; the right third holds the current card (prediction, method, results, calculation, variables, VRA, risk), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (inspected for P03 on 21 Oct; coded readout), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (coded copies, up to six on screen), `m6-volumetric-pipette-filler-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: bulb pipette with red filler; native aspect, rotated whole; the 50.0 mL, 20.0 mL and 10.00 mL transfers), `m5x-graduated-pipette-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: graduated pipette with red filler, at an angle; the 1.00 mL doses), `m6-volumetric-flask-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct; the tenfold dilution), `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png`, `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png`, `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` is not used (glacial ethanoic acid is a teacher stock, not vinegar).
